analysis.one_liner: Barred EPA from proposing carbon limits for existing power plants until new-plant limits were final.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved past committee: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and to its energy subcommittee the next day, it died with no hearing or vote when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited the EPA from proposing carbon emission limits on existing fossil-fuel power plants until the agency finalized and published limits for new plants. Because the new-plant rule was still unfinished, the practical effect would have been to postpone the limits covering the existing power fleet — the plants that actually produce today's power-plant emissions. It was referred to committee on introduction in December 2013 and never advanced again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal-fired utilities gain the most: the carbon standards the bill would have delayed fell hardest on existing coal plants, the core of the rulemaking it targeted. Fossil-fuel generators generally gained more time without binding federal carbon limits. Customers of coal-reliant utilities might have avoided some compliance costs passed through electricity rates in the short run, which is what the bill's supporters pointed to.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's single operative provision barred the EPA from proposing carbon standards for existing fossil-fuel-fired power plants under Clean Air Act section 111(d) until a standard for new plants under section 111(b) had been finalized and published in the Federal Register.

Since the new-plant standard was still unfinished at the time, this sequencing requirement would have kept the existing-plant rulemaking — the one covering the operating power fleet — off the table for as long as the new-plant rule took to finish.
The bill's framing as keeping the EPA 'honest' rested on the idea that the agency should finish new-plant standards before extending them to existing plants.

analysis.who_pays: The general public pays through a longer period of unregulated carbon emissions from the power sector — the emissions that drive climate change — plus the ordinary air pollution that comes with an aging plant fleet running under the old rules. These costs are spread thinly across everyone, while the gains are concentrated in one industry; the bill contained no ratepayer protection or environmental safeguard of its own.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via prolonged carbon emissions

drawbacks.text: The bill added no ratepayer protection, no environmental standard, and no safeguard of its own; its sole operative effect was to postpone the existing-plant rulemaking behind the unfinished new-plant rule.

The bar was temporary by design — it lifted once the new-plant standard was final — so its practical purpose was delay, and the delay fell on the rules covering operating plants rather than future ones.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill was procedural fairness: the title and sequencing design reflect supporters' argument that EPA should complete new-plant standards before applying them to the existing fleet, an objection that is coherent on its own terms even though the bill offered no substantive alternative.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The sequencing-fairness argument has surface appeal, but the bill would not have tightened any rule, protected any customer, or set any standard itself; its only measurable effect was added years of delay for the carbon rules covering the existing power fleet — the rules that matter most, since most power plants already exist. The gain would have flowed to coal and utility interests; the cost, in continued emissions, would have been spread across the public. As drafted, the costs clearly outweighed the procedural benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and to its energy subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held — it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced December 12, 2013 by Rep. David McKinley of West Virginia and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Referred on December 13, 2013 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 113th Congress — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended January 3, 2015.
The bill would have prohibited the EPA from proposing carbon standards for existing fossil-fuel power plants until a standard for new plants had been finalized and published in the Federal Register.
The bill attracted 9 cosponsors: 8 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA kept the freedom to move ahead with carbon limits on existing power plants, and the coal and utility interests that wanted those rules postponed did not get the delay written into law. People who wanted power-plant carbon standards came out ahead of the industries that sought to postpone them.

for.name: Rep. David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 12, 2013; it was referred to committee the same day.

for.name: Eight House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Capito (WV), Johnson (OH), Guthrie (KY), Cramer (ND), Stivers (OH), and Griffin (AR).

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor and was the bill's only Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee from the day of introduction with no markup, no committee vote, and no report to the floor for the rest of the 113th Congress.

against.name: Rep. Ed Whitfield
against.what_they_did: His subcommittee received the referral on December 13, 2013 and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: Speaker John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Never gave the bill House floor time; under House practice the majority leadership controls what reaches the floor, and the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The 9 cosponsors were 8 Republicans and 1 Democrat (Rep. Rahall of coal-producing West Virginia), and the bill died in committees run by the sponsor's own party — House Republican leaders never moved it.

industries.note: EPA's carbon rules for existing power plants were aimed hardest at coal-fired generation, and the bill would have postponed those rules until the separate new-plant rule was final — keeping coal plants unregulated longer and preserving coal's share of the electricity market at the cost of continued emissions.

The bill delayed the compliance costs that utilities warned would flow into customers' bills, an interest that partly overlaps ratepayers' pocketbooks — but the same delay meant more carbon and conventional pollution from the plants those customers live near.

Carbon standards push electricity generation from coal toward lower-carbon sources; postponing them slowed the market shift toward gas and renewables that would otherwise have come alongside lower emissions.
